questions.q: State the primary focus of marketing and the primary focus of selling as per NCERT Class 12 Business Studies.
questions.a: Marketing focuses on **customer needs and satisfaction**; selling focuses on **product and sales volume**. A wrong answer (e.g., "both focus on profit" or "marketing focuses on advertising") reveals the student conflates marketing with promotion or thinks both are synonymous with revenue generation, missing the customer-centric vs product-centric core distinction.

questions.q: A company manufactures electric scooters. The management says: "We have produced 10,000 units; now we need an aggressive sales team to push them through discounts and door-to-door canvassing before the festive season ends." Is this a marketing orientation or selling orientation? Justify using **two** distinguishing parameters.
questions.a: This is a **selling orientation**. Parameters: (1) **Starting point**: Production precedes customer research (they made 10,000 units first). (2) **Objective**: Short-term volume clearance via discounts/push, not long-term satisfaction. A wrong answer calling it "marketing because they want to sell" shows the student equates any sales activity with marketing, ignoring the sequence (needs first vs production first) and profit philosophy.

questions.q: Apply the marketing vs selling distinction to this scenario: A startup surveys 500 urban commuters about last-mile transport pain points, designs a foldable e-bike based on the top three unmet needs, prices it at ₹45,000 after competitive analysis, partners with metro stations for docking, and offers a 3-year battery warranty. Identify **three** marketing-oriented actions and explain why each is NOT selling.
questions.a: Three marketing actions: (1) **Surveying commuters first** — starts with needs identification (marketing starts before production; selling starts after). (2) **Designing based on unmet needs** — product development driven by customer insight (marketing focuses on satisfaction; selling focuses on existing product). (3) **3-year warranty & metro partnerships** — post-sale service and place strategy for long-term relationship (marketing scope is broad/integrated; selling scope ends at transaction). A poor answer lists "pricing" or "advertising" without linking to the *customer-first sequence*, indicating rote memorisation of 4Ps without grasping the philosophical shift.

questions.q:
Compare the profit philosophy of marketing vs selling using the formula:  
**Marketing Profit = f(Customer Satisfaction × Time)** vs **Selling Profit = f(Sales Volume × Margin)**.  
Analyse why a firm following selling orientation may report high quarterly profits but lose market share in 3 years, while a marketing-oriented firm may have lower initial margins but higher Customer Lifetime Value (CLV).
questions.a: Selling maximises **short-term profit per transaction** (high margin × volume push), often via discounts that erode brand equity and ignore post-purchase experience, leading to low repeat purchase and negative word-of-mouth. Marketing invests in **satisfaction-driven retention** (warranty, service, feedback loops), increasing CLV = (Average Purchase Value × Purchase Frequency × Customer Lifespan). Over 3 years, the marketing firm's compounding referrals and lower acquisition cost outweigh the selling firm's one-time spikes. A wrong analysis that only compares quarterly P&L misses the *time dimension* and *relationship asset* — a classic board exam trap where students treat profit as static.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: *"In a seller's market (high demand, low supply), selling orientation is superior to marketing orientation because customers will buy whatever is available."* Use the concepts of **caveat emptor vs caveat venditor** and **market dynamics** to defend or refute.
questions.a: **Refute.** Even in a seller's market, selling orientation is dangerous because: (1) **Markets shift** — when supply catches up (inevitable in competitive economies), the firm with no customer insight or loyalty loses instantly. (2) **Caveat venditor (let seller beware) is the modern legal norm** (Consumer Protection Act 2019) — ignoring satisfaction invites litigation and regulatory penalties. (3) **Reputation is path-dependent** — brands like Maruti Suzuki dominated India's seller's market in the 1980s *because* they invested in service networks (marketing), not just production. A student who agrees reveals a static view of markets and ignores the legal/ethical shift from caveat emptor to caveat venditor emphasized in NCERT.

questions.q: Create a 3-row comparison table for a **new Indian D2C skincare brand** showing how it would operate differently under selling vs marketing orientation across these dimensions: (a) Product Development, (b) Pricing Strategy, (c) Post-Purchase Engagement. Use specific actions (e.g., "survey 1,000 women on ingredient preferences" vs "copy competitor's bestseller").
questions.a:
| Dimension | Selling Orientation | Marketing Orientation |
|-----------|---------------------|------------------------|
| **Product Development** | Copy competitor's vitamin C serum; launch in 3 months | Survey 1,000 target users on skin concerns, allergies, packaging preferences; co-create formula with dermatologists; 12-month R&D |
| **Pricing Strategy** | Cost-plus 60% margin; heavy festive discounts to clear stock | Value-based pricing (willingness-to-pay analysis); tiered bundles (starter/loyalty); no deep discounts to protect brand equity |
| **Post-Purchase** | No follow-up; replace only if formal complaint filed | Free skin analysis after 30 days; personalized regimen app; loyalty points for reviews/referrals; easy returns |

A weak answer uses generic terms like "good quality" or "advertising" without *specific, measurable actions* tied to the orientation's logic, showing inability to operationalise the concept.
